title: Two kinds of giving up
hookLine: Arjuna's last question: is the holy life walking away, or letting go inside?
carry: tyaga: let go of the fruit, not the act
last: OM TAT SAT — OFFERED TO GOD.

cards: Go back to the very start of the Gita. The conch shells have sounded, the armies are drawn up, and Arjuna looks across at his grandfather and his teacher. His bow slips from his hand.

He sinks down in the chariot, and soon he's saying he'd rather live by begging than fight. India has an honored path that looks a little like that: the sannyasi, who leaves home, wears saffron and lives on what's given.
Seventeen chapters later, Arjuna asks his last question in the whole Gita, and it goes straight back to that moment: what does it really mean to give things up?

teach.b: Verse one: Arjuna asks to know the truth of two words. Sannyasa, renunciation, and tyaga, relinquishment. Both mean giving up.
Verse two: the wise say sannyasa is giving up actions done out of desire.

And tyaga, they say, is giving up the fruit of all actions. Verse three admits the wise disagree. Then Krishna gives his own view, verse five: sacrifice, giving and discipline should not be abandoned.
They should be done. They purify the wise. Verse six: but even these should be done without attachment, and without clinging to the fruit.
This is my firm conclusion. Then the three threads come back, now applied to giving up. Verse seven: quitting your proper duty out of confusion is tamasic.
Verse eight: quitting because it's hard, or you're afraid of the strain, is rajasic, and it gets you nothing.

Verse nine: doing your duty because it should be done, while letting go of attachment and the fruit, that's sattvic relinquishment. Verse eleven says it plainly. No one with a body can give up action completely.

teach.h: TYAGA: LET GO OF THE FRUIT.
teach.b: But the one who gives up the fruit of action is called a relinquisher. So the Gita's answer to the man who wanted to throw down his bow is not walk away. It's stay, act, and let go of the outcome.
This is karma yoga, the Gita's path of action, in its final form.
Hinduism honors the monk who leaves home, and it also says a parent, a student or a worker can truly give things up without leaving, by letting go of the fruit.

how: Hindu tradition honors sannyasis, renunciants who leave household life, and it also teaches householders the Gita's tyaga: doing one's duties fully while letting go of attachment to results.

o: letting go of the results while still acting
giving away all your money to the poor
leaving home and family for a monk's life

games.q: two kinds of giving up — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna's conclusion is to give up all action
verses 5–6: keep doing sacrifice, giving and discipline, without clinging to the fruit.
verse 11 says no one with a body can give up action completely
the relinquisher is the one who gives up the fruit.
quitting a duty because it's hard is called sattvic
verse 8: that's rajasic, and gains nothing.

games.q: you're Arjuna, at the start of the last chapter. you've wanted to drop your bow since chapter one. what's Krishna's firm conclusion?
o: keep acting, without attachment or clinging to the fruit.
act only when you're sure of the result.
games.why: verse 6: even sacrifice, giving and discipline should be done without attachment to the fruit. that's his firm conclusion.

practice: Think of one duty you'd love to quit, something that's yours to do but heavy, and notice whether the urge to drop it is confusion or fear of the strain.
Then, without deciding anything, picture doing it tomorrow, fully, but without needing it to turn out a particular way. Feel the difference in your shoulders; that's relinquishment.

wordCard.voice: Tyaga, relinquishment, letting go. Gita eighteen: sannyasa gives up actions; tyaga gives up the fruit, and Krishna's firm conclusion is to keep acting and let go of the fruit.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tyaga, relinquishment, letting go; in Gita 18, giving up the fruit of action, not the action.

carryVoice: Your line: tyaga, let go of the fruit, not the act. Stay on the field, and loosen the grip. Two hundred nineteen days, and counting.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.1–18.3 (sannyasa and tyaga; differing views)
Bhagavad Gita 18.4–18.9 (Krishna's conclusion; three kinds of relinquishment)
Bhagavad Gita 18.10–18.12 (no embodied being can give up action entirely)
